title: What is Kubernetes?
description: Understand the Kubernetes architecture, core concepts, and why container orchestration is essential.

data.text: As applications grow, you end up with dozens — sometimes hundreds — of containers running across many hosts. **Container orchestration** automates the deployment, scaling, networking, and lifecycle management of these containers so you don't have to manage them manually.
Think of it this way: Docker solved *how to run a single container*. Kubernetes solves *how to run thousands of containers across many machines and keep them healthy*.

terms.definition: A set of machines (nodes) managed by a single Kubernetes control plane.
The set of components (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd) that manage the cluster state.
A single machine (physical or virtual) that runs containers as part of the cluster.
The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes — one or more containers that share storage and networking.
The command-line tool used to interact with a Kubernetes cluster.

data.text: A Kubernetes cluster has two main parts: the **control plane** (the brain) that makes decisions about the cluster, and the **worker nodes** (the muscles) that actually run containers. In a managed offering like EKS, GKE, or AKS, the cloud provider manages the control plane for you.

data.title: Control plane components
data.text: etcd stores the entire cluster state as key-value pairs. The API server is the front door — everything goes through it. The scheduler assigns pods to nodes. The controller manager runs reconciliation loops that constantly move the cluster toward its desired state.

items: **Container runtime** — e.g., containerd or CRI-O, runs the container images.
**kubelet** — An agent that receives instructions from the control plane and reports node status back.
**kube-proxy** — Manages network rules and routing for services on the node.

data.text: Without orchestration, running containers in production means manual work: handling node failures, scaling during traffic spikes, rolling out updates without downtime. Kubernetes automates all of this and provides a declarative way to describe your desired state.

cards.title: Self-healing
cards.description: If a container crashes, Kubernetes restarts it. If a node dies, pods are rescheduled.

cards.title: Auto-scaling
cards.description: Scale applications based on CPU usage or custom metrics.

cards.title: Load balancing
cards.description: Distributes network traffic across pods for stability.

cards.title: Rolling updates
cards.description: Deploy new versions with zero downtime using rolling updates and rollbacks.

data.title: Exploring the cluster
data.content: Run these commands to see your cluster components in action.
data.code:
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get namespaces
kubectl get pods -A
kubectl describe node <node-name>

data.description: Use what you have learned to label the core components of a Kubernetes cluster.

List the worker node components and explain how they interact.

Run `kubectl get nodes -o wide` and note the node IPs and roles.
data.expectedOutcome: You can name every control plane and worker node component and explain its role in the cluster.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Kubernetes orchestrates containers across many machines, automating deployment, scaling, and recovery.
The control plane makes decisions; worker nodes execute them via kubelet, kube-proxy, and a container runtime.
Key resources: Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Ingress, and Namespace.
Use managed Kubernetes services (EKS, GKE, AKS) to avoid managing the control plane yourself.
data.takeaway: Kubernetes turns a fleet of machines into a single, self-healing application platform.
